title: ZK Foundations Lab — Build a Σ-Protocol Library

questions.question: In a Σ-protocol transcript (a, c, s), what is the verifier’s role for c in the interactive version?
options: Choose c uniformly at random from a large challenge space
Compute c as H(statement || a) mod q
Choose c to minimize the prover’s response size
Reuse the same c across sessions to simplify caching
questions.explanation: Interactive Σ-protocols rely on an unpredictable verifier challenge; Fiat–Shamir replaces this with hashing only in the non-interactive setting.

questions.question: What does “HVZK” (honest-verifier zero-knowledge) mean at a high level for a Σ-protocol?
options: There is a simulator that can produce accepting transcripts without the witness, for any challenge
The prover can convince any verifier even if the statement is false
The verifier learns the witness but cannot prove it to others
The protocol is secure even if the verifier chooses challenges adversarially after seeing s
questions.explanation: Special HVZK is demonstrated by a simulator that picks (c, s) and back-computes commitments so verification passes.

questions.question: Why must a Σ-protocol implementation validate that statement elements (like y) are in the intended subgroup?
options: Otherwise the verification equation may accept values outside the security model, enabling trivial or exploitable transcripts
Otherwise mod_inv will always throw an exception
Otherwise Fiat–Shamir hashing becomes non-deterministic
Otherwise the protocol becomes constant-time
questions.explanation: Group/subgroup membership is part of the statement domain; skipping it can invalidate soundness or allow cheating via small subgroups.

questions.question: In Schnorr, what does special soundness say you can do with two accepting transcripts that share the same commitment a but have c1 ≠ c2?
options: Extract the witness x efficiently
Simulate a transcript without knowing x
Compute a discrete log in any group in polynomial time
Derive a collision in SHA-256
questions.explanation: Two accepting responses to distinct challenges for the same commitment let you solve for x, which is why nonce reuse is catastrophic.

questions.question: A developer accidentally reuses the same prover nonce r across two sessions in Schnorr with challenges c1 and c2. What is the concrete consequence?
options: An attacker can recover the secret witness x from the two responses
Nothing; Schnorr remains secure as long as p is prime
The proof only fails to verify, but no secret is leaked
Only the commitment a is leaked, which is harmless
questions.explanation: Nonce reuse produces two equations s1 = r + c1 x and s2 = r + c2 x; subtracting and dividing yields x.

questions.question: In a Fiat–Shamir proof built from a Σ-protocol, which data must be hashed (at minimum) to derive c?
options: A domain separator plus the full statement and the commitment(s)
Only the response s (because it encodes everything)
Only the public parameters (p, q, g)
Only the witness x (to prove knowledge)
questions.explanation: The challenge must be bound to the statement and commitment(s), and domain-separated, so proofs can’t be replayed or transplanted.

questions.question: Chaum–Pedersen (DLEQ) proves that a single secret x is shared between (g1, y1) and (g2, y2). What changes compared to Schnorr?
options: There are two commitments (a1, a2) and verification checks two equations with the same (c, s)
The challenge c is no longer needed
The response becomes a pair (s1, s2) with different challenges
The protocol stops being a Σ-protocol
questions.explanation: DLEQ keeps the same transcript shape but uses a tuple of commitments and two verification equations tied to a single challenge and response.

questions.question: Why is an explicit, non-empty domain separator important when computing Fiat–Shamir challenges?
options: It prevents cross-protocol replay where the same transcript bytes would be interpreted as a proof for a different protocol/context
It increases the prime size p used by the group
It makes the proof constant-time automatically
It removes the need for subgroup validation
questions.explanation: Domain separation ensures that the same (statement, commitment) hashed under different protocols yields different challenges, avoiding transcript reuse across contexts.
